title: The one affront to justice in the Lucy Letby case that IS beyond doubt: Mail's veteran crime writer STEPHEN WRIGHT reveals the insider secrets that could change everything
text:
The case of Lucy Letby, the former nurse convicted of murdering seven babies and trying to kill another seven, returned to the front pages last week.
In a surprising turn of events, a Canadian neonatal expert announced at a press conference that “medical evidence does not support the murder (or murder attempt)” in any of the cases.
Dr. Shoo Lee, whose investigation had been summoned by the Prosecutor’s Office in the Letby’s 2023 trial (incorrectly, he says), summoned an independent panel of international experts to review each case individually.
They concluded that “in all cases, death or injuries were due to natural causes or simply to poor medical care”, which led many to question the validity of their convictions.
For my part, I think Letby guilty and denying his crimes. But the only opinion that must import is that of the Criminal Case Review Commission (CCRC), which has the power to refer to the alleged abortions of justice to the Court of Appeals. The body is considering the application of Letby, but if it has any hope of a quick decision, it will feel disappointed.
The case of Lucy Letby (in the photo), the former nurse convicted of murdering seven babies and trying to kill another seven, returned to the front pages last week.
The truth is that the CCRC is not suitable for its purpose, after a series of high profile errors and generalized accusations about its lack of professionalism and the endless time that even completes simple cases. In fact, a retired judge from the Superior Court told me recently that “it is a landfill for failed lawyers” and the “institutionally incompetent.”
His president, Helen Pitcher, was forced to resign last month after the Secretary of Justice, Shabana Mahmood, said she was “not suitable” to do the job. As head of CCRC, Pitcher won £ 95,000 a year for two days a week and had a disconcerting variety of simultaneous appointments. Sometimes he worked at his vacation home in Montenegro.
Given its history, the CCRC will take years to review the case of Letby before deciding whether there is a “real possibility” that the judges annul their convictions. Your legal team will not find breath in three CCRC controversies covered in detail by mail in the last 12 months.
The first involved Andrew Malkinson. He spent 17 years in jail for a violation he did not commit before his conviction was revoked in July 2023. The documents showed that another man’s DNA was found three years after he was unfairly imprisoned. But the CCRC did not act accordingly.
Another case refers to Clive Freeman, who has spent 35 years in prison for a murder that may not have happened, according to experts who reviewed the evidence. However, 12 months later, although it supposedly ‘accelerated’ his research because Freeman has cancer, the CCRC does not seem to reach a conclusion. Third, Peter Sullivan, the so -called ‘Beast of Birkenhead’, is ready to walk free after spending 38 years in jail for a terrible sexual murder he did not commit.
A late advance of DNA has provided “incontrovertible” evidence that Sullivan, a vulnerable man with learning difficulties, could not have sexually brutalized and mutilated, Diane Sindall, 21, in 1986. The CCRC failed to order new DNA tests In 2008 when Sullivan applied to make his case investigated. He has now been sent to the Court of Appeals.
So what has gone wrong in the besieged body?
With a budget of around £ 8 million, the CCRC has around 90 employees, of which 40 are case reviewers. But it is largely a body of “work from home” with its researchers scattered throughout the country.
Its objective is to complete at least 85 percent of cases within 12 months after receiving a application. But almost 100 cases are ‘hard’, which means they have been under review for more than 24 months.
The CCRC, which has the power to send alleged spontaneous abortions of justice to the Court of Appeals, is considering the letter of Letby to appeal its verdict
When asked how long the Letby probe would take, the CCRC told The Mail on Sunday that “it is not possible to determine how long will review this request.” He has also punished ‘speculation and comments … of parts with only a partial vision of evidence’ in the case of Letby.
Matt Foot, co -director of the appeal of charity, says: “The CCRC seeks skins to close the questions of a conviction shows that everything except independent is.”
Foot points out that, 26 years ago, a little known lawyer named Keir Starmer co -edited a book Deadriages of Justice: a review of the justice in error. “Given this,” says Foot, “you would expect that Starmer has the ambition to solve the disaster in the CCRC.”
But CCRC failures are so deep that an image change or a brand change will not be enough.
A completely new Appeals agency is needed, with a leadership team that includes a former main agent, former judges and lawyers. Together with those who must be managers to review cases with a deep knowledge of surveillance, law and forensics, something sadly is missing now.
Only with these changes can the public ensure that the integrity of the criminal justice system is being protected and that where there are serious reasons to challenge a conviction, the cases will be accelerated. If that will be the case of Lucy Letby or not, only time will say it.
